claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by kinetically trapping a homogeneous multimetal state before diffusion induces segregation.
Surface-energy-driven atomic diffusion can induce elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
Rapid nucleation followed by immediate quenching minimizes migration of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu are low-surface-energy constituents in the proposed nanoparticle system.
Suppressing Au and Cu surface migration preserves a well-mixed high-entropy structure rather than allowing phase separation.
A near-equimolar AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticle system with nuclei or crystallites approximately 2–6 nm in size is an example initial state for the test.
Immediate quenching can arrest the system before coalescence-driven diffusion begins.
High-temperature treatment causes coalescence of small AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The extent of coalescence and associated surface diffusion determines whether low-surface-energy elements have enough time to segregate.
Short growth times during rapid thermal processing kinetically trap multimetal nanoparticles in a homogeneous state.
Longer high-temperature exposure increases atomic mobility and permits surface-energy minimization.
In AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, phase separation progresses with increasing temperature through segregation of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles will have a more uniform elemental distribution and less Au and Cu surface enrichment than slowly processed nanoparticles.
A slower or prolonged high-temperature baseline will exhibit phase separation and Au/Cu surface segregation.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloy nanoparticles approximately 2–10 nm in size because surface effects dominate their diffusion kinetics.
The proposed mechanism need not apply to larger particles or bulk alloys because their diffusion and phase-separation dynamics differ.
The processing-time and temperature thresholds for kinetic trapping may vary with composition and particle size.
Precursor chemistry and solvent interactions may independently influence nanoparticle formation outcomes.
